Animal Farm. George Orwell's nineteen forty-five allegorical novella, a satirical fable in which farm animals rebel against their human master and establish a utopian society, only to have their revolution betrayed and corrupted by the pigs who seize power. Each character and event parallels the Russian Revolution and the rise of Stalinism. It is Orwell's bitterly clever warning that revolutionary ideals can be perverted into tyranny by those who capture the narrative and rewrite history.

Published in nineteen forty-five after World War Two, Orwell wrote it during the war but faced resistance because the Soviet Union was an Allied power. The allegory was considered too inflammatory. The animals of Manor Farm rebel against Mr. Jones, who stands for Tsar Nicholas, and establish Animal Farm based on Seven Commandments. But the pigs, especially Napoleon and Snowball, quickly assume leadership and begin to concentrate power. Napoleon, representing Joseph Stalin, uses propaganda and violence to eliminate his rival Snowball, who represents Leon Trotsky. Then he rewrites history and the Commandments to justify his rule and privileges.

The narrative is deceptively simple: farm animals talking and working and rebelling. But every detail is coded. The pigs' ascent, the corruption of ideals, the falsification of history, the complicity of the other animals. The final commandment is the fable's most piercing political irony. The pigs alter the original all animals are equal to all animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others.

Orwell uses a naive narrator who doesn't fully grasp events and a fairy-tale tone. The gap between surface innocence and dark reality creates devastating satire. Animal Farm became the most widely read anti-totalitarian allegory of the twentieth century, required reading in schools as a warning against tyranny and propaganda. George Orwell was the author of this most bitterly satirical and most perfectly executed fable. Nineteen Eighty-Four is Orwell's fuller, more direct dystopian vision, where Animal Farm is allegory while 1984 is brutal realism. The book employs political satire at its finest, mocking totalitarian ideology by embodying it in animal characters. It concerns totalitarianism itself, showing how revolutionary ideals are corrupted into totalitarian control and propaganda. The Soviet Union is the historical target, with the Bolshevik Revolution and Stalinist regime as the fable's referent.
